caption_hook: Iowa has dust hills, crystal-filled geodes, an ancient coral sea and a sliver of billion-year-old rock.

layers.name: LOESS HILLS
layers.what: Ice-age winds blew fine silt off glacial floodplains and piled it hundreds of feet deep along the Missouri River. The soft, fine dust still forms steep, ragged bluffs.
layers.bonus: Only China has loess deposits this deep, which makes the Loess Hills globally rare.

layers.name: KEOKUK FORMATION
layers.what: A warm, shallow sea left muddy limestone full of sea lilies. Over time, quartz crystals grew inside hollow pockets in the rock, forming the geodes that collectors crack open.
layers.bonus: The geode is Iowa's official state rock, picked by the legislature in 1967.

layers.name: CEDAR VALLEY LIMESTONE
layers.hook: A coral reef under the Corn Belt
layers.what: A tropical sea covered Iowa and grew reefs of coral and sea creatures. At Devonian Fossil Gorge near Iowa City, floods in 1993 and 2008 scoured away the soil and exposed the old seafloor.
layers.bonus: Fossil Gorge reveals tens of thousands of fossils in one flat limestone surface.

layers.name: GALENA DOLOMITE
layers.what: Cracks in this seafloor rock filled with lead ore. Miners dug it from the bluffs above the Mississippi, and the town of Dubuque grew around the mines.
layers.bonus: Dubuque is named for Julien Dubuque, who mined lead here in the 1780s.

layers.name: SIOUX QUARTZITE
layers.what: Ancient river sand was buried and squeezed into rock-hard pink quartzite. It pokes out of the prairie only in Iowa's far northwest corner, where it is among the state's oldest visible rock.
layers.bonus: Deeper down, a billion-year-old failed rift runs hidden under central Iowa.
